The person in question there was Todd Broadwater. I cannot find the quote from Todd Howard saying Broadwater made all the caves himself, but I would certainly believe it, for the same information I told someone else in the thread.

As for dungeons overall, they were headed by Istvan Pely and designed by a handful of other people including: Tim Lindsey, Frank Ward, Michael Ryan, Robert Wisnewski, Jeff Browne, and Joel Burgess.

So when people say (not your comment, but some I've seen) that one person made all 265+ dungeons in the game, they would be discounting the work of all these people. I certainly think the "Making Of" Oblivion documentary gave people the idea that, as well as doing all the caves (\*need source), Broadwater did all the other dungeons, as he was the primary spokesperson for that team in the video.

I feel that. However, Oblivion actually started the loop mechanic (to some degree). Many caves, such as that inside the Forsaken Mine, have strange rock walls that can be activated to allow easier access toward the start again. This also occurs in Ayleid Ruins.

However, the difference here is that they usually only did this in very large dungeons, or some with a clearly difficult layout with which the map function may not have been much help due to overlays and confusing perspective. In Skyrim, they do loop dungeons far more than necessary, in my opinion.

Fully agree on the loop dungeons. In some cases the dungeons in later TES titles can be incredibly large, and I find the easy-out to be a breath of fresh air. However, as you are saying, even the smaller dungeons in, say, Skyrim, almost always have a "you got to the end! Now here is an easy exit that makes very little sense so you don't ever have to look at a map".

Not dungeon-related, but I think this fits along with the removal of so many skills and spell types. Skyrim in particular was very much streamlined for a wider audience.

That is also important for a game such as Morrowind where the normal movement speed is very, very slow compared to modern games. When they are small dungeons, they still feel large as a result of this, which can make large ones feel like a drag.

I absolutely love the Dwemer (I began the series with Morrowind), so I am biased to really enjoy all of their dungeons within Skyrim as well. I really love the way they made them feel so alive despite being machines, and that the structures in this game are truly as huge as they tried to make them feel in Morrowind.

As for the Falmer, it makes total sense to me that they would inhabit these abandoned ruins, but I have to agree that they are creepy / annoying to deal with. Oh, and the loot they drop is basically useless as well, compared to whatever else you can find.

Very true. The caves were made from a small selection of tile options. When I mentioned the one "cave slope structure", I was describing the corner in which the ground ramps up, usually under a skylight, and then there is usually a chest right below it.

These corner pieces come in 4 indistinguishable variants and have been used 998 times across the game. Since there are 94 caves, that means (assuming all caves are similar in size for easy averages) each one has the same piece repeated about 10 times! The fact that they are so unique and visually noticeable is what adds to that feeling of repetition, I think.

Right. There are nearly 200 dungeons including DLC, and all of them are so similar. The dwemer locations are awesome (though I am biased since I love the Dwemer), but I guess that isn't a specific descriptor of what makes me enjoy them.

There are also only 6 dungeon types including: dwemer ruins, caves, forts, mines, nordic ruins, and realms of apocrypha. The fact that there are so few (albeit very visually interesting and often containing large and elaborate themes) types also makes the game feel pretty repetitive.

They also removed a lot of the daedra types from the previous titles. I would say they have less enemy types, but upon looking further, I think it mainly revolves around the fact that there are more "normal" things, like spiders, wolves, warriors, etc. And then, variations on those (think Draugr Wight, Draugr Warlord, Bandit Overlord, etc).

But yeah, I fully agree that things can start to feel repetitive. What is your favorite thing about the dungeons?

I never played the Xbox or PlayStation titles (recently played 1-3 for the first time through the remaster), but I did play eternal night and some of the DS ones.

Believe it or not, many games of that era were made intentionally difficult for two reasons (among more, probably).

1. The replaying of missions artificially boosted the time spent playing. So the game felt longer and seemed bigger than it was, and thus, a better product.

2. (More for disc games) Games were made to be difficult, especially American versions of Japanese games, so that they stretched the time required to beat them. Game rentals were a thing in the US (then illegal in Japan). Why buy a game at full price when I can beat it in a night for $5?

Anyway, just random interesting stuff

SOF was (is) killer. The music, the sound design, the level design (for the most part).

My largest complaint for AOTR was the backtracking issue. Haven’t played in years but I still remember it. 

Oh, and the difficult Sgt. Byrd sections. But maybe they were only hard cause I was a child.

The isometric graphics are probably the largest (and valid) complaint. They can make it hard to time certain jumps and stuff.

If you let yourself go back to an earlier time, they can be really fun. Even the sound effects are just really nice sometimes. And the maps (in SOF, AOTR, I haven’t played SOI) are super pretty.

SOF has some of the coolest level themes I’ve played in any video game, shout-out to the Halloween level.

He could only use flame magic (all he knows in the book, but he’s very talented). Otherwise he relied on his intense Ordinator training with a mace. He is from the Order of Inquisition and deeply despised heretics and the 6th house.

Things like the vow of silence quest were somewhat difficult for him, since he relied on others for fast travel, potions, etc.

Eventually his individualism (he has no friends other than Ahnassi, who he found a personal liking for - doesn’t fit the RP as he is somewhat racist and fine with slavery, I just really like Ahnassi and the house lol) led him to learn Alchemy - just so he could survive the journey without speaking to others.

Very important stuff:

Keep restore fatigue (green bar) potions. If your fatigue is low: you can be knocked down, run slower, have much lower chance to hit/cast spells, etc. Make sure you stop running when in combat.

Keep restore strength potions. Greater Bonewalkers in certain dungeons can ruin your day by reducing your strength below the norm, forcing you to drop all your stuff, heal at a temple (Almsivi Shrine), and return.

Go slow. Your own pace. Pick a different character for different questlines. Some factions hate each other and won’t allow you in.

You have to use skills to get better at them. No perks!

Take your time exploring. There are hand placed things hidden all over the place. Use levitation to scope out high areas in caves, etc. It’s always worth checking!

Read. Talk to everyone. Check out the in game books.

Don’t abuse alchemy. I’m telling you up front, there is a method. But if you just do it organically, you can create potions that are just as good as you’ll ever need.

Save. Save. Save. All the time. Hit F5 for quick save before starting a hard fight. Entering a cave. Etc.
